articles.title: Here’s How to Make a Time Capsule That’ll Last Your Family for Generations
articles.content:
It’s hard to forget the day your elementary school class buried a time capsule—the excitement of knowing that someday future students and teachers, or maybe even you and your classmates at your 30-year reunion, would get a glimpse of what your life was like. Maybe you tucked in a fact sheet listing your favorite foods, video games, school subjects and closest friends, or a letter to your future self predicting flying cars. Or maybe you and your best friend stuffed a coffee can with friendship bracelets, the names of your crushes and a mixtape of your favorite songs.
These days, it may seem as though a time capsule wouldn’t be worth making when a quick online search can turn up old yearbook photos, newspaper archives and videos of just about anything you ever played with or listened to. But nothing compares to holding the real thing: the soft crease of a handwritten letter, the rough, snaggly hair of a vintage Barbie doll, the crackling of a well-worn single on a record player. Objects that were actually there at the time carry a look and feel no screen can match, and that’s exactly what a time capsule preserves.
So if you’re wondering how to make a time capsule as a grown-up, here’s the good news: It’s not only easy—it’s also even more meaningful the second time around, especially when you do it with your family. That’s because it’s a literal snapshot of who you are right now: the jokes everyone repeats at dinner, what the kids want to be when they grow up, what a gallon of milk costs, and the way Grandma signs her name. They’re exactly the kind of everyday details that slip away over the years and that future generations most want to know … that is, if they’re able to decode cursive!
And the timing couldn’t be better. The holidays bring multiple generations together under one roof, and everyone is already in a reflective, year-in-review mood. “The people holding the undocumented memory are physically present, and that’s the part you can’t recover later,” says Steven Lazaroff, founder of the genealogy research marketplace GeneoHub.
So how do you make one of these for yourself? To find out, I spoke with Lazaroff and genealogy expert Lisa Louise Cooke, author of The Genealogist’s Google Toolbox and host of the Genealogy Gems Podcast. Read on to learn how to make a time capsule your family will treasure (and actually open), plus simpler ways to capture your loved ones’ stories each year.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more knowledge, family, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
People have been leaving messages for the future for centuries, but the oldest known time capsule in the United States dates back to 1795, when Samuel Adams, Paul Revere and Colonel William Scollay placed a box beneath the cornerstone of the Massachusetts State House. When it was opened at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, in 2015, it held coins dating as far back as 1652, newspapers, a copper medal of George Washington and a silver plaque thought to be engraved by Revere. Pretty cool, right?
That said, the modern time capsule took shape in the 1930s. The man often called “the father of the modern time capsule” is Thornwell Jacobs, the former president of Oglethorpe University in Georgia. In 1935, while researching ancient civilizations, he was struck by how little accurate information had survived. So he set out to preserve a record of 20th-century life for the people of the future. The result was the Crypt of Civilization, a 20-foot-long room beneath the university’s Phoebe Hearst Hall. (Fun fact: The room was once a swimming pool.) Inside are more than 640,000 pages of microfilm, newsreels, recordings, a set of Lincoln Logs, a Donald Duck doll and even a machine designed to teach English to whoever finds it. It was welded shut on May 28, 1940, and isn’t scheduled to be opened until May 28, 8113.
Jacobs’s plan made headlines when he announced it in 1936, and the term time capsule was coined soon after, when Westinghouse Electric & Manufacturing Company began preparing a capsule of its own for the 1939 New York World’s Fair. Sealed on Sept. 23, 1938, and buried about 50 feet underground at the fairgrounds, the bullet-shaped cylinder holds more than 100 items, including seed samples, microfilm and a handwritten message from Albert Einstein. It’s slated to be opened in 6939.
“Time capsules are unique in that they are curated by the family itself and not a third party like a governmental agency,” says Cooke. “Each item has special meaning. It’s a way to speak to the future about what you valued in your present.”
Lazaroff sees the value from the other side: His business helps families piece together their history from records. “My job is reconstructing context that no longer exists,” he says. “I can find you a birth date. I can’t tell you what your great-grandmother’s kitchen smelled like.” A time capsule, he explains, is your one chance to put in that context on purpose.
“Decide the open date first,” says Lazaroff. “Everything else follows from it.” How long the capsule stays sealed shapes what you put inside, what kind of container you need and how much explaining your future selves will need.
For a long-term family capsule, 20 to 25 years is the sweet spot, according to Lazaroff. Instead of choosing a round number, tie the opening to a life event, like “when your youngest turns 30.” Events get remembered, he says—dates don’t. If you’re thinking even further out, keep in mind that past 50 years, you may not be around to explain what everything means, so the capsule has to make sense entirely on its own.
If you have young kids, consider doing both a short-term and a long-term capsule. A one-year capsule opened on a birthday or next Thanksgiving shows kids that the payoff is real. Children under about age 10 can’t really imagine 25 years from now, Lazaroff explains, so a long-term capsule on its own can feel like an abstraction to them.
Knowing how to make a time capsule that survives the years comes down to a few key decisions. Here’s how to do it, step by step.
Your capsule’s biggest enemies are moisture, light, temperature swings, pests and acid, says Lazaroff. Look for containers and supplies labeled acid-free, lignin-free and Photographic Activity Test (PAT)–passed (meaning the material won’t react with photos). Inert plastics like polypropylene and polyethylene are ideal. Avoid PVC entirely, since it gives off gases that can ruin photographs within a couple of decades. And skip cardboard, which is acidic and attracts pests.
On a budget? Lazaroff says a military-surplus steel ammo can with a rubber gasket works well indoors. It’s sealed, pest-proof and light-proof, and it typically costs around $30.
Cooke likes a more decorative approach: a lovely box secured with a lock and displayed on a high shelf. “[It] not only serves as a reminder of the excitement of the opening day to come, but it can also be easily brought along in the case of a move,” she says. If you go this route, line it with acid-free folders or sleeves, and keep it out of direct sunlight.
A holiday gathering is the perfect time to fill your capsule. Lazaroff suggests waiting until right after a big meal, “when nobody wants to move.” Then try a few of these ideas.
When you write your questions, focus on personal experiences and feelings, not the news of the day, which is easy to look up later. Cooke recalls reading the autobiography of her husband’s great-great-grandmother. “I was captivated by her description of her daily chores (so different from today) and how she felt about them, much more than [her] discussing the facts of the end of the Civil War,” she says.
The best time capsules mix the meaningful with the mundane. Here’s what our experts recommend.
Certain items quietly destroy themselves … and sometimes everything around them. Skip or work around the following, says Lazaroff.
Before you seal anything, let all the contents sit indoors for a few days to make sure they’re completely dry, and add a few silica gel packets. Don’t make the container airtight unless everything inside is bone-dry, warns Lazaroff, or “you’ve built a mold incubator.”
Then label the outside in large letters: “FAMILY TIME CAPSULE. DO NOT DISCARD. OPEN [insert date],” along with a name and contact information.
Burying a time capsule may be the classic move, but both experts advise against it. Ground moisture, freeze-thaw cycles and tree roots can all damage the contents. And people move. Cooke’s former next-door neighbor learned this the hard way. Twenty years earlier, he had buried a capsule in his backyard containing his father’s World War II medals and some family gold. When he moved, he forgot it. He came back six months later, and the new owners graciously let him dig, but he never found the capsule.
Instead, keep your capsule in an interior closet on a main or upper floor, off the ground and out of the light, Lazaroff recommends. Avoid the attic (temperatures swing too much) and the basement (humidity and flood risk). “If you wouldn’t be comfortable sitting in that spot for a year, neither will your photographs,” he says.
If your family is set on burying it, Lazaroff suggests three layers of protection: the archival container inside, a sealed waterproof barrier around it, and a rigid outer vault rated for burial. Never put it directly into soil. Choose high ground with good drainage, away from anywhere that might be built on, paved or planted. Most important, mark the spot above ground with something permanent, like a plaque, an engraved paver or a stone. “The marker is the entire ballgame,” he says.
The biggest threat to a time capsule is being forgotten. “Almost no capsule is lost to decay,” says Lazaroff. “They’re lost to being forgotten and thrown out.” An unlabeled box is easy to toss during a move or an estate cleanout. Here’s how to keep yours on everyone’s radar.
When the big day arrives, Cooke suggests transferring the items into a glass-sided display case so everyone can enjoy them. Have everyone at the opening sign a card and take a group photo, then add those to the display. Then you can reuse the capsule and start the next one!
If a sealed box feels like too much, a simple annual tradition can capture your family’s story just as well, and you get to enjoy it along the way. Try one of these.

If you go this route, line it with acid-free folders or sleeves, and keep it out of direct sunlight.

2. Get the whole family involved

A holiday gathering is the perfect time to fill your capsule. Lazaroff suggests waiting until right after a big meal, “when nobody wants to move.” Then try a few of these ideas.

  • Pass a notebook around the table with a single question in it. Let everyone answer in their own handwriting. “The handwriting matters as much as the answer,” says Lazaroff.
  • Let the grandkids play interviewer. Cooke suggests having grandchildren hand out paper and pens and pull prearranged questions from a bowl. They ask a grandparent the question, the grandparent writes the answer, and the grandchild places it in the capsule.
  • Record the oldest relative telling one story. Just put a phone on the table. “You’re not making a documentary—you’re capturing a voice,” Lazaroff says.
  • Give the teenager the camera. They get to document the day.
  • Write down everyone who was in the room. Include full names and the date. “In 50 years, that page will matter more than anything else in the box,” says Lazaroff.

When you write your questions, focus on personal experiences and feelings, not the news of the day, which is easy to look up later.   • Labeled photographs printed on real photo paper. Name every person in every photo, using a soft pencil or photo-safe pen, never a ballpoint or Sharpie, which can bleed through. “Every genealogist alive has a box of unidentified faces,” says Lazaroff.
  • Handwritten letters from each family member. The handwriting itself becomes a keepsake.
  • Everyday items. These could be a school lunch menu, a transit pass or a grocery receipt (photocopied). “Historians treasure the mundane because big events are documented everywhere,” Lazaroff says. “Nobody saved what bread cost.” 
  • Kids’ creations. Think: fridge drawings, letters to Santa, report cards and homework assignments.
  • A printed family tree. It should include both current family members and ancestors, so the connections are clear. Cooke suggests a free tool like MyHeritage’s Family Tree Builder. You can also add notes, like the oldest ancestor you met in person or which relative taught you something important.
  • A list of what you don’t know. Lazaroff suggests writing down family mysteries, like: “We never learned her mother’s maiden name.” Open questions tell a future researcher exactly where to dig.
  • Copies of key family records—never originals—laser-printed onto acid-free paper. Write where each record came from, including the archive (e.g., a county clerk’s office, a state’s vital records office, a church parish or a historical society), reference number and date. “A photocopy with no source is nearly useless,” says Lazaroff. “A copy with a reference number is a treasure map.”
  • A one-page profile of each person. Include their name, dates (birth, death, marriages), where they’ve lived, what they do, one story they tell and one opinion they hold. If you record audio, include a printed transcript too.
  • An index page listing every item and why it’s there. Objects without an explanation become trivia.

4. Know what to leave out

Certain items quietly destroy themselves … and sometimes everything around them. Skip or work around the following, says Lazaroff.

  • USB drives, SD cards and DVDs. The media itself degrades, and the technology to read it may not exist in 20 years. “Digital media formats have changed countless times just in our own lifetime, making analog a much more attractive option,” says Cooke. If you want to include digital photos or videos, print the most important ones.
  • Newspapers. They’re highly acidic, and the acid spreads to everything they touch. Photocopy articles onto acid-free paper instead.
  • Thermal receipts (the shiny kind). They fade within a few years. Photocopy them.
  • Inkjet prints. Again, these fade badly. Laser prints and true photo prints last much longer.
  • Rubber bands, paper clips, staples, tape and lamination. Rubber rots, metal rusts and stains paper, and lamination traps acid against a document permanently.
  • Anything organic or liquid. These items can attract pests or leak.
  • Original documents you might need, like birth certificates or passports. “If you need that birth certificate for a passport next spring, you’ve locked it away,” Lazaroff says.

5. Prep before sealing

Before you seal anything, let all the contents sit indoors for a few days to make sure they’re completely dry, and add a few silica gel packets. Don’t make the container airtight unless everything inside is bone-dry, warns Lazaroff, or “you’ve built a mold incubator.”

Then label the outside in large letters: “FAMILY TIME CAPSULE. DO NOT DISCARD. OPEN [insert date],” along with a name and contact information.

Avoid the attic (temperatures swing too much) and the basement (humidity and flood risk). “If you wouldn’t be comfortable sitting in that spot for a year, neither will your photographs,” he says.

If your family is set on burying it, Lazaroff suggests three layers of protection: the archival container inside, a sealed waterproof barrier around it, and a rigid outer vault rated for burial. Never put it directly into soil. Choose high ground with good drainage, away from anywhere that might be built on, paved or planted. Most important, mark the spot above ground with something permanent, like a plaque, an engraved paver or a stone. “The marker is the entire ballgame,” he says.

How to ensure you won’t forget your time capsule

The biggest threat to a time capsule is being forgotten. “Almost no capsule is lost to decay,” says Lazaroff. “They’re lost to being forgotten and thrown out.” An unlabeled box is easy to toss during a move or an estate cleanout. Here’s how to keep yours on everyone’s radar.

  • Label it clearly. Make sure it’s emblazoned with the open date and a contact name, as described above.
  • Tell at least three people across two generations. You want backup in people, not just in notes.
  • Set a recurring calendar reminder for the open date. Also mention the capsule in your will.
  • Photograph the capsule and where it’s stored, then email those photos to yourself and two relatives. Email archives tend to survive house moves better than paper.
  • Take it with you when you move. Lazaroff suggests writing “TAKE ME” right on the box.
  • Register it. The free International Time Capsule Registry, created with the International Time Capsule Society, is designed to help people track down capsules decades later.
  • Keep it in sight. This is where Cooke’s on-display approach shines: A capsule on a shelf is much harder to forget than one buried in the backyard.

What should you do when it’s finally time to open it?

When the big day arrives, Cooke suggests transferring the items into a glass-sided display case so everyone can enjoy them. Have everyone at the opening sign a card and take a group photo, then add those to the display. Then you can reuse the capsule and start the next one!

What’s a low-key way to capture your family each year?

If a sealed box feels like too much, a simple annual tradition can capture your family’s story just as well, and you get to enjoy it along the way. Try one of these.

  • Ask the same three questions every year. Pick a date, like Thanksgiving or Christmas, and ask everyone the same questions, then write down the answers. “After 10 years, it’s extraordinary, and it takes 20 minutes,” says Lazaroff.
  • Host a label-the-photos night. Once a year, pull up that year’s photos and name everyone in them. “Unglamorous, and worth more to your descendants than any capsule,” Lazaroff says.
  • Write a birthday letter to each child every year. Seal them, and hand over the whole stack when they turn 18.
  • Print 10 photos a year. Physical prints are the only format Lazaroff would bet on still being viewable in 50 years.
  • Make a year-in-review photo book. Cooke suggests print-on-demand services like Shutterfly or Lulu to turn the year’s photos into a hardcover book. Give copies as holiday gifts, or let each family member order their own.
  • Set up a digital photo frame with an album for each year. Cooke suggests putting it on display during the holidays as a year in review. You can even include photos of handwritten notes.
  • Record one story from your oldest relative every year, and transcribe it. “This is the one with a real deadline, and the one families always mean to get to,” says Lazaroff.
  • Write wishes for your future self. Have everyone do this at Thanksgiving dinner, seal them in an envelope and read them aloud next year.
  • Start a family tree. If the capsule sparks curiosity about your ancestors, building a family tree is a natural next step.

No. The U.S. government’s official advice remains the same: Three days’ worth of supplies is sufficient. Other countries also give recommendations of days, not months. Well, there is something, and it’s right on my computer—and yours. On Windows PCs, it’s the Performance tab within your computer’s Task Manager app. On Macs, it’s called the Activity Monitor. Both apps track computer operations that are running in the background, as well as storage capacity and other key performance issues. They’re filled with valuable information that can help you figure out why your tech is bogging down for no apparent reason.

What, exactly, do they tell you?

Both the Windows Performance tab and the Mac Activity Monitor capture tons of processes, but the five main ones that are helpful for diagnosing a slow computer are:

  • CPU usage: Your computer’s Central Processing Unit runs applications and software, performs calculations and generally acts as the “brain” of your computer. High CPU usage isn’t always bad, but if it’s high during certain operations, it could be a clue as to why your computer is dragging.
  • Memory (RAM): Random-access memory is your computer’s short-term memory. When you open an app, stream a movie or play a game, RAM is where your computer stores the data and files that the CPU needs right away while the application is in use.
  • Disk space: Your disk drive or hard drive is your computer’s long-term memory, where files, photos and other things that are not needed while applications are running are stored. But it can also store shorter-term files, especially if the RAM is inadequate.
  • Network processes: This information doesn’t pertain to your physical computer, per se, but a slow network connection can definitely be a reason it isn’t working as fast as it should on processes that require the internet.
  • GPU usage: This is your graphics processing unit, aka graphics card. It’s what’s needed to quickly render videos, movies, games and other graphics-heavy applications, as well as process your computer’s overall visuals.

How do you find these menus?

It’s easy, but there are few ways to get there, depending on your operating system.

Open the Performance tab on Windows computers

  • Use the Start button: Right-click on the Start button, select Task Manager and then navigate to the Performance tab on the left (it looks like a line graph).
  • Use the taskbar: Right-click on an empty part of the taskbar, select Task Manager and navigate to the Performance tab.
  • Use keyboard shortcuts: Hit Cntl + Shift + Esc at the same time to bring up the Task Manager directly. Alternatively, you can use Cntl + Alt + Del, and then select Task Manager from the menu.

Open the Activity Monitor on a Mac

  • Use Spotlight search: Hit the Command button and the space bar, then type in Activity Monitor and hit return. You can also find Spotlight by clicking the magnifying glass in the top right corner of your screen.
  • Use Finder: Open Finder on your dock, then go to the toolbar across the top and select Go > Utilities > Activity Monitor. If Finder is not in your dock, click any empty space on your desktop and the Finder toolbar will appear.
  • Use the Apps icon: Select the Apps icon from your dock, then type in Activity Monitor and hit return. Apps is a dedicated apps launcher within Spotlight that rolled out with the Tahoe update, but if you are running an older version you’ll know it as Launchpad.
  • Use a keyboard shortcut: Hit Fn + Shift + A to bring up the Apps search directly.

What are you looking for?

There’s a lot of information in the Performance tab and Activity Monitor, and some of the more technical fixes are beyond the scope of this article. But you can start with some basic troubleshooting. When your computer is running slowly, open the Task Manager or Activity Monitor and be ready to jot down what you see.

Here are some top line things to look for and correct or research further.

High CPU usage

Temporary spikes are not necessarily concerning, but if your CPU is consistently running near the maximum, the fan is loud or your computer is just plain slow, click over to the Processes tab on a PC (right above the Performance tab) or click the CPU column on a Mac. Close any resource-heavy apps that you’re not using, then restart and recheck.

Update or reinstall apps that continually use too many resources, and disable apps that start up automatically so they’re not constantly running in the background. You can also try cleaning your computer’s fan and vents with compressed air.

Low disk space and RAM

Heavy RAM usage often indicates too many things are running at once. Close apps you’re not using as well as browsers and/or excessive tabs that are open. Today’s browsers are much bigger resource hogs than they used to be, constantly loading and running videos, background scripts and ads. Restart. If the problem persists, consider adding more RAM.

If disk space is low, get rid of files, videos and images you no longer need. Close apps you’re not using, clear up space by running your computer’s disk cleanup function, and consider upgrading to a solid state drive instead of an older hard drive.

High GPU usage

If your Activity Monitor or Performance tab shows high graphics-card usage, close video games and graphics-heavy apps and browsers. Restart your computer. If you continue to see that the GPU usage is high, you may need to update your graphics card.

Network problems

If you’re having network connectivity problems, it’s always worth it to stop any downloads or heavy streaming activities that could be hung up. Restart your computer, make sure your router and/or modem are online, and run a speed test from your internet provider.

What else can you do to fix a slow computer?

It’s worth trying some general fixes. Here are more tips that can help speed up your PC or Mac.

  • Restart your computer. Yes, it sounds basic, but restarting does give your computer a little refresh by clearing out temporary files and closing background processes that might be hung up.
  • Close any programs you’re not using. Close extra tabs, browsers and apps. Change your startup settings so you don’t have a lot of programs running in the background that you’re not using.
  • Scan for malware. Viruses and malware can cause slowdowns, so run an antivirus program like Microsoft Defender Antivirus. For a Mac, Apple’s protection is built in and runs automatically.
  • Keep your computer updated. When your computer says you have software or operating-system updates available, download them. Recommended patches and anti-virus updates not only keep you safe from hackers—they can speed up a slow computer too.

articles.title: Need to Calm Down ASAP? Here’s How to Activate Your Vagus Nerve in 3 Minutes or Less and Keep Stress at Bay
articles.content:
I can usually tell when my anxiety has crossed from “I’m worried about this” into “I can’t seem to let this go” because the logic stops logic’ing. I might know, rationally, that whatever I’m spiraling about probably isn’t as catastrophic as it feels, but I still end up fixating on it until I’m dizzy and hyperaware of every thump in my chest.
That disconnect is frustrating … but it’s also potentially useful. The thing is, anxiety isn’t just spinning thoughts or sweaty palms; it’s happening in both your mind and your body at once. And that means you may be able to work on the physical side of the response instead of simply waiting for your brain to magically become reasonable.
The vagus nerve is one of the key players in that mind-body connection, helping your brain communicate with organs throughout your body and playing an important role in shifting you out of a stress response. If anxiety can send that whole system in one panicked direction, there’s a lot of interest in whether you can work from the body up to help steer it back toward calmer waters, and there’s some pretty convincing science behind it.
To learn how to stimulate the vagus nerve, I spoke with Richard Gevirtz, PhD, a psychology professor at the California School of Professional Psychology at Alliant University, and Christopher Austelle, MD, a board-certified psychiatrist and a clinical assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University. Read on to learn how to work with your nervous system to calm down a whole lot faster.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more wellness, science, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
The vagus nerve is one of the body’s major communication routes. Though we colloquially refer to it in the singular, we actually have two vagal nerves. They travel from the brainstem through either side of the neck and then into the chest and abdomen, passing the heart, lungs and digestive tract along the way.
Comprised of more than 200,000 nerve fibers, the vagus nerve is also the primary nerve involved in the parasympathetic nervous system, explains Gevirtz. Quick biology refresh: Your sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems help manage many of the things your body does automatically. The sympathetic side helps mobilize you when something requires action, while the parasympathetic side helps bring things back toward rest and recovery afterward. Gevirtz describes the parasympathetic system as the “rest, digest and restore” side.
You need both: The goal isn’t to stay relaxed all the time—it’s to be able to ramp up when you need to, then settle again.
The vagus nerve can help calm some of the physical changes that happen when you’re anxious. As a major pathway of the parasympathetic nervous system, it helps regulate heart rate, breathing and digestion, as well as helps your body return toward rest after a stress response.
During stress, Gevirtz explains, sympathetic activity normally increases while parasympathetic activity temporarily drops, a process sometimes called vagal withdrawal. That shift helps your body gear up to respond; once the demand has passed, the balance should move back toward rest and recovery. You can see part of that process with every breath. Your heart rate naturally rises slightly as you inhale and falls as you exhale, a pattern the vagus nerve helps regulate. Those beat-to-beat differences contribute to heart rate variability, or HRV.
A 2022 meta-analysis published in Psychiatry and Clinical Neurosciences found that people with anxiety disorders tended to have lower parasympathetic activity at rest. In other words, the part of the nervous system that helps you wind down may be less active in people with anxiety. But that doesn’t necessarily mean the vagus nerve itself isn’t working properly.
For the most part, it does. Your vagus nerve isn’t a muscle that becomes weak because you forgot to exercise it, and it generally doesn’t need to be “reset.”
The problem, Gevirtz says, can be spending long stretches of time in that withdrawn state when life—and let’s be honest, the world—feels like a lot. He compares the nervous system to a thermostat: What matters isn’t making it stronger, but how readily it can shift when circumstances change.
The things you can do at home don’t directly stimulate the vagus nerve in the same way medical treatments do. (More on that below.) Dr. Austelle, who researches vagus nerve stimulation, says these techniques are better understood as behaviors that “influence” vagus nerve function.
That influence can happen in a few different ways. Here are five techniques to try.
“One of the techniques with the most evidence and the most convincing evidence is slow breathing,” Dr. Austelle says.
